## Overview

The Mosuo, also called Moso, Mosso, Musuo, or Na, are an ethnic group living in the Hengduan mountains of China's Yunnan and Sichuan provinces. Approximately 40,000 people belong to the group, many living in the Yongning region around Lugu Lake, as well as in Labai, Muli, and Yanyuan. The Mosuo are culturally distinct from the Nashi, although the Chinese government claims that the two groups are the same. They speak Na, also called Narua or Mosuo, a Naish language of the Naic group within the Sino-Tibetan language family. Their folk-culture significance lies especially in their matrilineal house organization, walking marriages, oral religion, agricultural lifeways, distinctive household arrangements, and continuing efforts to preserve their language, script, and religious traditions.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*No named textile or pattern tradition is documented in the sources used. The sources state that some older Mosuo women know how to use looms to produce cloth goods.*

### Clothing & dress

Mosuo children dress alike before the coming-of-age ceremony. At the age of thirteen, girls receive skirts and boys receive trousers in ceremonies known respectively as the “skirt ceremony” and the “trouser ceremony.” After coming of age, women may have a private bedroom called a *flowering room*.

### Architecture

Mosuo homes consist of four rectangular structures arranged in a square around a central courtyard. The first floor houses livestock, including water buffalo, horses, geese, and poultry, and contains the main cooking, eating, and visiting areas. The second floor is commonly used for storage and bedrooms. Mosuo houses are organized around the *Awo*, a corporate house group of about twenty people. Buildings, land, and livestock are owned collectively by the house. The hearth is described as the heart of the Awo and combines the worship of nature, ancestors, and spirits. Behind it is a stone slab called *guo zhuang* in Chinese and an ancestral altar where household members leave food offerings before meals.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 When an *Ah mi* passes her duties to a female successor, she gives her the keys to the household storage, signifying the transfer of property rights and responsibility.

## Music & performance

 They do describe praise songs in connection with Mosuo religion: the vast majority of praise songs involve maternal love, reflecting the importance of the guardian mother goddess and the feminine description of mountains, lakes, and the surrounding environment.

Religious performance is central to Daba practice. *Daba* priests conduct rites and ceremonies, perform exorcisms, bless families, assist the spirits of the dead, and preserve oral traditions. They may enter a trance and converse with spirits. Daba priests are called upon during naming ceremonies, coming-of-age ceremonies, funerals, and special events such as the Spring Festival. Buddhist monks also perform religious services, including prayers of thanks, prayers for the dead, education, and counsel. During funerals, Buddhist monks preside over cremation while Daba priests direct the soul of the deceased to *Seba'anawa*, the afterworld of the Na.

## Festivals & rituals

The Mosuo coming-of-age ceremony occurs at the age of thirteen and is one of the most important events in a child’s life. Before it, children dress alike and are restricted from aspects of Mosuo life involving religious rites. Afterward, girls receive skirts and boys trousers. Women can then have a private *flowering room* and, after puberty, may begin inviting partners for walking marriages.

Walking marriage, also called *tisese*, is a prominent Mosuo form of marriage. Partners live with their respective extended families during the day. At night, a man may visit a woman’s house with permission and return to his own household in the morning. Children belong to the mother’s family and are raised with major support from the mother’s extended household, especially her brothers.

Funerals are arranged by men. Families send men to assist with preparations, while *Dabas* and *Lamas* recite prayers. Caskets are small and square, and the deceased is placed in a fetal position so that the person can be reborn in the next life. During cremation, a decorated horse is led around the fire to help carry the deceased’s spirit away. Afterwards, relatives and friends pay their last respects and wish the deceased an easy journey to the ancestral land.

The hearth is honored before each meal, including when tea is served, through an offering of food at the ancestral altar. Tibetan Buddhist holidays and festivals are attended by the Na community. The sources also mention the Spring Festival.

## Foodways

Mosuo subsistence is primarily agrarian. Farming includes raising livestock and growing grains and potatoes. Livestock include yak, water buffalo, sheep, goats, and poultry. The sources also mention corn, sunflowers, soybeans, pumpkins, beans, oats, buckwheat, flax, and rice. Rice became a major crop during the mid-twentieth century and makes up more than half of annual production.

Meat is important in the diet. Because refrigeration is lacking, meat is preserved by salting or smoking. Mosuo are especially known for preserved pork, which may be kept for ten years or more. Pigs have several social functions: pork is served to guests, offered at funerals, and used as payment or reimbursement. Pork is also described as a symbol of wealth and a kind of currency.

The Mosuo produce a local alcoholic grain beverage called *sulima*, which is compared in the sources to strong wine. It is drunk regularly and offered to guests, at ceremonies, and at festivals. They fish on Lake Lugu and use land-based fish traps, but do not use motorboats. Dogs are valued members of the family and are never killed or eaten. During initiation into adulthood, Mosuo adolescents pray before the family dogs.

## Oral tradition & literature

Daba is an oral religion handed down through generations by word of mouth and is described as holding much of the Na people’s culture and history. Daba priests preserve the oral tradition associated with the Na and their *Awos*. Their religious duties include conducting rites, performing exorcisms, blessing families, assisting deceased spirits, and caring for the sick.

The Mosuo formerly used a hieroglyphic script written on animal hides. The sources state that only thirty-two characters and an oral memory remain, although the community of Youmi has led to the discovery of more than four hundred new characters and more than three hundred sacred texts belonging to the Mosuo people. Sacred stories were written by Daba priests and preserved in the script, which could be written into clothes, letters, scrolls, and books to secure blessings.

A cultural crisis has emerged because past Chinese government policies made being a Daba priest illegal. There are now few remaining priests, most of them old men. After the restrictions ended, the Na began training young people as Daba priests again. Efforts are also underway to develop a full written form of the Mosuo language.

## Language & religion

Na, also called Narua or Mosuo, belongs to the Naish subbranch of the Naic group of the Sino-Tibetan languages. Yongning Na is spoken in Yongning Township, Ninglang County, Lijiang, Yunnan, China, and has three tonal levels. Lataddi Narua has two tonal levels. Narua’s default word order is agent–object–verb, and sentence topics can be marked with *jjo*.

The Mosuo formerly used a hieroglyphic script, but today use Han script for daily communication. Tibetan script may be used for religious purposes. Daba is the holistic religion and worldview of the Na and includes animism and shamanism. The Na worship natural spirits, ancestors, a mother goddess, and the mountain goddess Gemu. Daba priests are men who live in their mother’s Awo. Tibetan Buddhism has influenced Daba over the centuries, especially the Gelug school. Buddhist practices and Daba ceremonies coexist, and Tibetan Buddhism has become predominant in recent years.
